newsitem.title: UK: Funds transfers seen if any EMU state unrest.
newsitem.headline: Funds transfers seen if any EMU state unrest.

text.p: Social unrest in countries which belong to a European single currency could spark an exodus of overnight funds to safer parts of the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), a British corporate treasurer said on Thursday.

"If a country begins to look as though it is getting into a distressed situation, then it is likely corporate treasurers will make sure their overnight money is not in that country," David Creed, group treasurer of Tate & Lyle Plc, told a conference on EMU.

"So as usual markets could well accelerate the concern which is causing the market to show differentiation (between EMU member states) and this destabilising effect, instead of being on the currency, would start to be a credit risk."
Creed said such an exodus of funds would be in response to the risk that an EMU member might have to leave the union quickly, taking with it foreign company funds deposited within its jurisdiction.

Gareth Jones, managing director for treasury and wholesale banking at Abbey National Plc, said there were questions about what would happen to euro currency debt if a country quit EMU and reverted to its own national currency.
However, he said lenders could threaten to grant no more loans to the country concerned if it tried to repay these debts other than in euros.

Jones said the growing importance of credit risk meant European sovereign credits would not all trade at the same levels after EMU. He pointed to the example of Canada whose provinces had differing ratings.

He said strong companies in countries like Belgium and Ireland should have the chance to borrow at better terms than their governments after EMU, since a nation's credit rating would no longer constitute a ceiling rating for a country's corporate borrowers.
